question.text: A landlord owns a non-domestic rented property in England currently at EPC Band D. Under the government's proposed MEES tightening (2021 BEIS consultation), assuming the regulations are laid as proposed, on what date does the property first become illegal to let, and what is the minimum EPC band required to re-let?

answer.text: 1 April 2027. Minimum EPC Band C required from that date. Subsequent tightening proposed to Band B by 1 April 2030. As of June 2026 the regulations remain proposed — the government's formal response to the 2021 consultation has not been laid. Action: plan for 2027 cliff-edge regardless of slip risk.

question.text: A landlord in England rents out a domestic property at EPC Band F. Under current MEES domestic regulations, what date did the property first become illegal to let, and what enforcement penalty range applies?

answer.text: 1 April 2020 — minimum EPC Band E required for ALL existing domestic tenancies in England and Wales (new tenancies became subject from 1 April 2018). Maximum civil penalty £5,000 per breach, capped at £5,000 per property within a 12-month period. Local Weights and Measures Authorities enforce. Note: the proposed tightening to Band C for new tenancies from 2028 (then all by 2030) has not yet been laid as of June 2026.
answer.citation: Energy Efficiency (Private Rented Property) (England and Wales) Regulations 2015, regulation 36; Trustpilot Government enforcement guidance

question.text: A new-build housing developer in England is laying foundations in autumn 2026. The Future Homes Standard takes effect when, and what change in regulated energy performance does it require compared to current Building Regulations Part L 2021?

answer.text: The Future Homes Standard comes into force on 24 March 2027. Transitional provisions: work is not caught where a building notice, initial notice or application for building control approval with full plans was given before 24 March 2027 AND the building work commenced before 24 March 2028. A developer laying foundations in autumn 2026 under an earlier application is therefore likely to remain under Part L 2021, subject to meeting the commencement condition on that individual building. The standard requires approximately a 75-80% reduction in regulated CO2 emissions against the 2013 Part L baseline, delivered mainly through low-carbon heating (heat pumps) and improved fabric, with gas boilers no longer specifiable in new dwellings. Part L 2021 was the interim step delivering roughly 31%.
answer.citation: The Future Homes and Buildings Standards: Building Circular 01/2026; Approved Document L Volume 1 (2025 edition)

question.text: Under the EU EPBD recast (2024/1275/EU), all non-residential buildings must be zero-emission by what date, and what does the EU define as a zero-emission building?

answer.text: All NEW non-residential buildings owned by public authorities must be zero-emission by 1 January 2028. All NEW non-residential buildings (regardless of ownership) by 1 January 2030. Existing non-residential buildings must achieve a defined energy-performance threshold by 2030 (top 16% worst-performing) and 2033 (top 26%). A zero-emission building is defined as: very high energy performance (lowest national class), zero on-site combustion of fossil fuels for heating, primary energy demand met by renewables on-site or nearby (district), or grid-supplied renewable energy.
answer.citation: Directive (EU) 2024/1275 on the energy performance of buildings (EPBD recast)

question.text: When does the UK ban on installation of new gas boilers in existing buildings take effect, and what is the policy mechanism?

answer.text: There is currently NO confirmed UK-wide ban date for replacement gas boilers in existing buildings. The 2021 Heat and Buildings Strategy committed to a phase-out from 2035, but the September 2023 announcement weakened this to remove the policy commitment. Current trajectory: 80% boiler-replacement market share for heat pumps by 2035 via the Clean Heat Market Mechanism (CHMM) — boiler manufacturer obligation introduced from 2025, originally with quota and fine of £6,000 per heat-pump shortfall but later softened. Action: do not assume a hard ban; check current policy at any specific decision point.

question.text: A building owner is told their property must comply with ESOS Phase 4. What is the compliance deadline, what does the regime require, and what penalties apply for non-compliance?

answer.text: ESOS Phase 4 deadline is 5 December 2027 (4-yearly cycle; Phase 3 was December 2023, but for Phase 3 the Environment Agency extended to June 2024). The regime applies to UK 'large undertakings' (>250 employees OR >£44m turnover and >£38m balance sheet). Requires: energy audits covering ~90% of total energy consumption, including buildings, transport, and industrial processes. Phase 4 introduces a mandatory action plan and annual progress reporting (new requirement). Civil penalty up to £50,000 plus £500 per day continued non-compliance. Lead assessor must be ESOS-registered.

question.text: A commercial landlord acquires a property with an EPC Band E. The EPC was issued 9 years ago. When does the EPC formally expire under current rules, and what triggers a requirement to issue a new EPC?

answer.text: An EPC is valid for 10 years from the date of issue under the Energy Performance of Buildings (England and Wales) Regulations 2012. New EPC required when: (a) the building is sold, (b) the building is rented to a new tenant, (c) a building is newly constructed, (d) a building is materially altered such that the existing EPC no longer reflects its energy performance. For MEES compliance, landlords must hold a valid EPC at the point of letting — re-letting beyond the EPC expiry is not allowed without a fresh EPC. So in this case: EPC formally expires at year 10 (1 year away), but action triggered immediately by acquisition for any new letting.
answer.citation: Energy Performance of Buildings (England and Wales) Regulations 2012; MEES Regulations 2015

question.text: Building Safety Act 2022: which buildings are classified as Higher Risk Buildings under the regime, and what does the gateway-2 process require before construction can start?

answer.text: Higher-Risk Buildings under the Building Safety Act 2022 are buildings at least 18 metres in height or with at least 7 storeys AND containing at least 2 residential units. (HRBs in occupation also include care homes and hospitals with these height thresholds.) Gateway 2 requires the Principal Designer and Principal Contractor to submit a full set of detailed building safety information to the Building Safety Regulator (HSE-led) BEFORE construction can begin. BSR has 12 weeks to determine. The application must include a competence declaration, structural and fire safety strategy, and a building control approval application. No construction begins without Gateway 2 approval. Gateway 3 then applies before occupation.
answer.citation: Building Safety Act 2022; Higher-Risk Buildings (Procedural) (England) Regulations 2023; Building Regulations etc. (Amendment) (England) Regulations 2023

question.text: An owner of a 1980s commercial office is told they must comply with TM44 air-conditioning inspections. What is the inspection trigger, frequency, and consequence of non-compliance?

answer.text: TM44 / EPBR requires inspection of air conditioning systems with effective rated output >12 kW. Inspection must be carried out every 5 years by an accredited energy assessor. The first inspection is required within 5 years of installation OR within 5 years of the property changing hands (whichever earlier). Inspection report must be lodged on the central register (Landmark for England/Wales). Failure to comply: £300 civil penalty per breach (per system), with continuing breaches escalating. The inspection identifies efficiency improvements; recommendations are advisory not mandatory.

question.text: A non-domestic landlord in Scotland (NOT England) is informed that Scotland's MEES equivalent is changing. What is the Scottish regime and timeline?

answer.text: Scotland has its own Section 63 Climate Change (Scotland) Act 2009 regime called 'Assessment of Energy Performance of Non-domestic Buildings Regulations 2016' (commonly Section 63). It applies to non-domestic buildings over 1,000 m2 (excluding very small properties). On sale or new letting, an Action Plan must be lodged identifying improvement opportunities with paybacks under 7 years. Compliance with the Action Plan within 3.5 years (with extensions possible). Penalties up to £1,000 per breach. Scotland is also consulting on a Heat in Buildings Bill which may introduce minimum standards for non-domestic by 2028 — currently delayed but expected.

question.text: A London office development planned for completion in 2027 is told it must demonstrate a Whole Life-Cycle Carbon Assessment (WLCCA). What policy mandates this, what's the threshold, and what's the metric used?

answer.text: London Plan 2021 Policy SI 2 requires WLCCA for major referable developments (residential schemes 150+ units OR over 30 m tall OR specified non-residential thresholds). Assessment methodology per GLA Guidance using RICS Whole Life Carbon Assessment for the Built Environment Professional Statement. Metric is kgCO2e/m2 GIA over 60-year reference study period (modules A1-A5, B1-B5, C1-C4, D as informational). Boroughs increasingly adopting similar thresholds in local plans (e.g. Westminster, Camden). Action plan must show reductions against business-as-usual reference building.

question.text: Under the F-Gas Regulation (UK retained EU 517/2014 as amended), R410A refrigerant: what is its GWP, what are the key 2025-2030 servicing/charging restrictions, and what are common drop-in alternatives?

answer.text: R410A has a GWP of 2088 under IPCC AR4, which is the basis used by the UK retained F-Gas Regulation (EU 517/2014); the AR5 value is 1924. Because 2088 sits below the 2500 threshold, virgin R410A remains permitted for servicing existing equipment rather than being caught by the 2500-GWP servicing ban. Placing-on-the-market restrictions bite on new equipment instead: single split air-conditioning systems containing less than 3 kg of F-gases with GWP of 750 or more have been prohibited since 1 January 2025, which rules R410A out of most new small splits. Common lower-GWP replacements are R32 (GWP 675 AR4) and R454B. Reclaimed and recycled R410A remains available for servicing, with volumes constrained by the phase-down quota.
answer.citation: F-Gas Regulation (EU) 517/2014 as retained and amended, Annex I and Annex III; IPCC Fourth and Fifth Assessment Reports

question.text: The Streamlined Energy and Carbon Reporting (SECR) framework applies to which UK organisations, what must they report, and via what mechanism?

answer.text: SECR applies to: (a) quoted companies (UK incorporated and listed on a main exchange), (b) large unquoted companies (meeting 2 of 3: >£36m turnover, >£18m balance sheet, >250 employees), and (c) large LLPs (same thresholds). Report energy use (kWh) for UK operations covering electricity, gas, and transport, plus associated scope 1+2 GHG emissions and intensity metric. Reported via the Directors' Report (quoted companies and LLPs) or the Strategic Report (large unquoted). Methodology recommended: HM Government Environmental Reporting Guidelines. Includes principal energy efficiency actions taken in the year.

question.text: Under the UK Heat Network (Metering and Billing) Regulations 2014 (HNMBR), what triggers an obligation on a heat supplier, and what are the key obligations for heat-network operators serving 'final customers'?

answer.text: Heat Network (Metering and Billing) Regulations 2014 apply to any heat supplier providing heating, cooling, or hot water to final customers via a heat network. Notification to Office for Product Safety and Standards (OPSS) — the current HNMBR regulator since 2020 (Ofgem is the future regulator under the Energy Act 2023, not yet in effect). Key obligations: install building-entry heat meters where cost-effective; install consumption-allocation meters in multi-occupancy buildings where cost-effective and technically feasible; bill final customers based on actual consumption at least annually; provide clear billing information. OPSS enforcement; civil penalties per Schedule to the Regulations.

question.text: A school in England with multiple buildings totals 8,500 m2. Under the Display Energy Certificate (DEC) regime: what triggers DEC requirement, what's the validity, and what advisory report accompanies it?

answer.text: DECs are required for buildings over 250 m2 'occupied by a public authority and frequently visited by the public' under the EPB Regulations 2012. The school qualifies. The DEC must be displayed in a prominent place visible to the public. Validity: 1 year for buildings >1,000 m2 (so this 8,500 m2 building needs annual DEC); 10 years for 250-1,000 m2 buildings. Accompanied by an Advisory Report (10-year validity) detailing energy-efficiency recommendations. Civil penalty £500 for failing to display + £1,000 for not having an Advisory Report. Lead assessor must be accredited DEC assessor.
answer.citation: Energy Performance of Buildings (England and Wales) Regulations 2012; Trading Standards / Landmark register

question.text: A landlord in England lets a domestic property currently rated EPC Band F. They received a tenant complaint in May 2026. Under the current domestic MEES regime, what is the minimum EPC rating required, when did this become enforceable for all existing tenancies, and what is the maximum civil penalty per property for non-compliance?

answer.text: Minimum EPC Band E is required. The standard applied to new tenancies and renewals from 1 April 2018 and to all existing domestic tenancies, including continuing ones, from 1 April 2020. Civil penalties, per property: up to GBP 2,000 where the property has been let in breach for less than three months; up to GBP 4,000 where it has been let in breach for three months or more; up to GBP 1,000 for registering false or misleading information on the PRS Exemptions Register; up to GBP 2,000 for failing to comply with a compliance notice. A publication penalty may be imposed alongside any of these. The maximum total is GBP 5,000 per property. Enforcement is by the local weights and measures authority.

question.text: A commercial landlord in Manchester owns an office building rated EPC Band F. They argue MEES does not apply because the lease is a 99-year ground lease. Under non-domestic MEES, what is the current minimum EPC rating, when did this become enforceable for all existing leases, and what tenancy length triggers the regulations?

answer.text: Current minimum is EPC Band E. For new lettings/renewals it applied from 1 April 2018; for ALL existing non-domestic leases (continuing tenancies) it has applied since 1 April 2023. MEES applies to tenancies granted for a term of more than 6 months but less than 99 years — so a 99-year ground lease is OUTSIDE scope (and tenancies of 6 months or less without right of renewal also excluded). Maximum penalty is the GREATER of £5,000 or 10% of rateable value (capped £50,000) for breaches under 3 months; greater of £10,000 or 20% of rateable value (capped £150,000) for breaches of 3+ months, plus publication penalty. Proposed tightening: Band C by 1 April 2027 and Band B by 1 April 2030 remains the 2021 BEIS consultation position — government response/regulations not yet laid as of June 2026.
answer.citation: Energy Efficiency (Private Rented Property) (England and Wales) Regulations 2015 (SI 2015/962), Part 3

question.text: A domestic landlord cannot improve their EPC F-rated property to Band E because three quotes show works would cost £12,000. Under the domestic MEES 'high cost' exemption, what is the cost cap, what evidence is required, and how long does the exemption last?

answer.text: The domestic 'cost cap' exemption is £3,500 INCLUDING VAT (set in March 2019; before that, the original 2015 regulations used a 'no upfront cost' principle via Green Deal — abolished). If the cheapest recommended improvement to reach Band E exceeds £3,500 inc VAT, landlord must install all improvements possible within the £3,500 cap, then register the 'all relevant improvements made' exemption. Evidence required: three installer quotes for the recommended measure(s) from the EPC, plus EPC itself. Exemption registered on the PRS Exemptions Register (publicly searchable) is valid for 5 years, after which landlord must reassess. Exemption is NOT transferable on sale — new landlord must re-register. Note non-domestic uses a different '7-year payback' test (Regulation 27), not a £ cap.
answer.citation: Energy Efficiency (Private Rented Property) (England and Wales) Regulations 2015 as amended by SI 2019/595

question.text: A non-domestic landlord claims a MEES exemption because installing recommended cavity wall insulation would not pay back within an acceptable period. What is the specific payback test used for non-domestic MEES, how is it calculated, and who enforces non-domestic MEES?

answer.text: The non-domestic '7-year payback test' (Regulation 27): a recommended improvement need not be installed if the expected energy savings over 7 years are LESS than the cost of installation. Calculation: (annual energy savings × 7) compared against installation cost (inc VAT). Energy savings use prevailing energy prices at the date of EPC/assessment, with savings estimated by a qualified person. If test fails for a measure, that specific measure can be excluded; landlord must still install all measures that DO pass the 7-year test. Exemption registered on PRS Exemptions Register, valid 5 years, not transferable on sale. Enforcement is by the LOCAL WEIGHTS AND MEASURES AUTHORITY (Trading Standards) of the local authority — not the EPC register operator or DESNZ. They can issue compliance notices (request info within 1 month) and penalty notices within 18 months of breach.
answer.citation: Energy Efficiency (Private Rented Property) (England and Wales) Regulations 2015, Regulation 27 and Part 5

question.text: A landlord owns a Grade II listed Victorian terrace let on an AST. The EPC is Band G. They claim MEES does not apply because the building is listed. Is this correct, and what categories of property are genuinely outside scope of domestic MEES?

answer.text: INCORRECT as a blanket claim. Listed status does NOT automatically exempt a property from MEES. A listed building is exempt from the requirement to have an EPC only where compliance with minimum energy performance requirements would 'unacceptably alter character or appearance' — and DESNZ/MHCLG guidance is clear this is not automatic; many listed buildings DO require EPCs and are subject to MEES. The landlord would need evidence (e.g. conservation officer view) that all relevant improvements would unacceptably alter character. Genuinely out-of-scope categories: (1) properties not legally required to have an EPC (e.g. places of worship, temporary buildings ≤2 years, some industrial sites with low energy use, stand-alone buildings <50m²); (2) tenancies of 6 months or less with no right of renewal and tenant not in occupation >12 months; (3) tenancies of 99+ years; (4) certain HMO arrangements where no EPC is required on the dwelling as a whole. Registered exemptions (cost cap, consent, devaluation) are time-limited and DO require the EPC — they differ from being out of scope entirely.
answer.citation: Energy Efficiency (Private Rented Property) (England and Wales) Regulations 2015; Energy Performance of Buildings (England and Wales) Regulations 2012; DESNZ Domestic Private Rented Property MEES Guidance

question.text: A designer is working on a new residential development with south-facing single-aspect flats in London. Under Approved Document O (Overheating), what compliance routes are available, what are the key thresholds for the simplified method, and when did it become mandatory?

answer.text: Approved Document O came into force 15 June 2022 (transitional: exempt if building notice/initial notice/full plans deposited before 15 June 2022 AND work commenced before 15 June 2023). Two compliance routes: (1) Simplified Method — limits glazing area as % of floor area depending on cross-ventilation availability and location (high-risk locations include central London and Manchester city centre, where stricter glazing limits apply; e.g. 11% for single-aspect south-facing in high-risk areas with restricted openings, vs higher % allowances elsewhere). Requires free-area openings sized to ≥ specified % of floor area. (2) Dynamic Thermal Modelling using CIBSE TM59 methodology — predicted hours of overheating must not exceed TM59 criteria (≤3% occupied hours >26°C in bedrooms 22:00-07:00; living rooms ≤3% hours exceeding adaptive comfort threshold). Single-aspect south-facing flats in central London will almost always require TM59 modelling — simplified method rarely passes. Security/noise constraints on openable windows must be considered.
answer.citation: Approved Document O: Overheating (2021 edition, in force 15 June 2022); CIBSE TM59:2017

question.text: A developer is delivering a new residential block with 50 flats and 60 parking spaces. Under Approved Document S, what are the EV charging requirements, what exemptions apply, and what minimum charge-point specification is required?

answer.text: Approved Document S came into force 15 June 2022 (transitional: exempt if building notice/initial notice/full plans deposited before 15 June 2022 AND work commenced before 15 June 2023). For new residential buildings with associated parking: every dwelling with an associated parking space must have one EV charge point. Minimum specification: 7 kW (single-phase, Mode 3, Type 2 socket or tethered). For the scenario (50 flats, 60 spaces): each dwelling with a space gets a charge point, and remaining spaces must have cable routes (ducting/passive infrastructure) for future installation. Exemption: if cost of connection upgrade exceeds £3,600 per dwelling, requirement reduces to cable routes only (this is the principal cost cap). Mixed-use and non-residential have different thresholds (1 in 5 spaces active for new non-residential ≥10 spaces, plus passive). Caveat: charge-point smart functionality requirements sit under Electric Vehicles (Smart Charge Points) Regulations 2021, separate regime.
answer.citation: Approved Document S: Infrastructure for the charging of electric vehicles (2021 edition, in force 15 June 2022); Electric Vehicles (Smart Charge Points) Regulations 2021

question.text: A contractor is installing MVHR in a new airtight dwelling targeting 3 m³/h·m² at 50 Pa. Under Approved Document F Volume 1 (2021), what whole-dwelling ventilation rate applies, what commissioning and testing requirements apply, and what indoor air quality monitoring is required?

answer.text: Under Approved Document F1 (2021 edition, in force 15 June 2022): for highly airtight dwellings (≤5 m³/h·m² at 50 Pa) continuous mechanical ventilation (System 3 MVHR or System 4 MEV) is effectively required — natural ventilation (System 1) is not suitable below ~5 m³/h·m². Whole-dwelling minimum ventilation rate is the greater of (a) 0.3 l/s per m² of internal floor area, or (b) a rate based on number of bedrooms (1 bed = 19 l/s, 2 bed = 25 l/s, 3 bed = 31 l/s, 4 bed = 37 l/s, 5 bed = 43 l/s). Commissioning: airflow rates must be measured at every terminal and recorded on a commissioning sheet given to building control AND the occupier; flow tolerance typically ±15% of design. New 2021 requirement: indoor air quality monitoring (CO2, humidity, VOCs) is required only in certain non-domestic settings under F2 — for dwellings the focus is commissioning records and occupier information. Caveat: ADF was updated in tandem with Part L 2021; FHS-era ADF, published alongside the Future Homes Standard which comes into force 24 March 2027, may tighten further — confirm current edition.
answer.citation: Approved Document F Volume 1: Dwellings (2021 edition, in force 15 June 2022); Building Regulations 2010 Regulation 42 (commissioning)

question.text: A self-builder submitted full plans for a new detached house on 1 May 2023 under Part L 2013 and commenced foundations on 1 August 2024. Building control queries whether the project must now comply with the Part L 2021 uplift. What does the transitional provision say, and what is the consequence if the start-of-work test fails?

answer.text: Part L 2021 (ADL Volume 1, 2021 edition) came into force 15 June 2022. Transitional provisions (Building Regulations etc. (Amendment) (England) Regulations 2021): an individual building is exempt if (a) building notice/initial notice/full plans were deposited before 15 June 2022 AND (b) work on that individual building commenced before 15 June 2023. Crucially, this was tightened from previous uplifts: transitional applies per-building (not per-site), and 'commencement' for transitional purposes means meaningful work on that specific building (excavation of foundations / laying of foundations), not just site-wide enabling works. In this scenario: full plans were deposited 1 May 2023 — already AFTER 15 June 2022, so the transitional does not apply regardless of commencement date. Project must comply with Part L 2021 (target ~31% CO2 reduction vs Part L 2013 baseline, higher fabric standards e.g. roof U-value 0.11 W/m²K notional, wall 0.18). Consequence of failure: building control will refuse completion certificate; remedial works to bring fabric/services up to 2021 standard required; potential enforcement notice under s.36 Building Act 1984.
answer.citation: Approved Document L Volume 1 (2021); Building Regulations etc. (Amendment) (England) Regulations 2021 (SI 2021/1391); Building Act 1984

answer.text: Gateway 1 applies at the PLANNING APPLICATION stage for Higher-Risk Buildings (≥18m or ≥7 storeys AND ≥2 residential units). It requires the applicant to submit a Fire Statement demonstrating that fire safety matters have been incorporated into the planning proposal (site layout, access for fire appliances, water supplies, escape routes, external wall construction). The Health and Safety Executive (acting as the Building Safety Regulator) is a statutory consultee on planning applications for HRBs and must be consulted by the Local Planning Authority. Gateway 1 has been in force since 1 August 2021 (ahead of Gateways 2 and 3). Failure to submit a compliant Fire Statement is grounds for the LPA to refuse or treat the application as invalid.

question.text: A Principal Accountable Person manages an occupied 22-storey residential tower in Manchester. Under the Building Safety Act 2022, what is the Safety Case Report requirement, when must it be produced, and what penalties apply for failing to register or comply?

answer.text: All occupied HRBs in England had to be registered with the Building Safety Regulator between 6 April 2023 and 1 October 2023 (registration deadline). The Principal Accountable Person must prepare a Safety Case Report identifying and assessing building safety risks (spread of fire and structural failure) and demonstrating that all reasonable steps have been taken to manage them. Failure to register an occupied HRB is a criminal offence: summary conviction up to 2 years' imprisonment and/or unlimited fine for the PAP. Occupying an unregistered HRB is also an offence. question.text: An architect is being appointed as Principal Designer under the Building Regulations dutyholder regime for an HRB project. What competence must they demonstrate, what standard underpins the assessment, and what is the personal liability risk?

answer.text: Under the Building Regulations etc. (Amendment) (England) Regulations 2023 (in force 1 October 2023), the Principal Designer for Building Regulations purposes (distinct from the CDM 2015 Principal Designer, though often the same person) must have the skills, knowledge, experience and behaviours (SKEB) to plan, manage and monitor design work and coordinate matters relating to compliance with Building Regulations. For HRBs, competence must be demonstrated against BS 8670-1:2021 (overarching framework) and PAS 8671:2022 (Principal Designer-specific competence). The client has a duty to make reasonable enquiries to confirm competence before appointment. Personal liability: failing to comply with dutyholder duties is a criminal offence under the Building Act 1984 (as amended) — up to 2 years' imprisonment and/or unlimited fine. Extended limitation period under s.135 BSA 2022 increases retrospective liability to 30 years for completed dwellings.

question.text: A UK-incorporated company with 280 employees, £55m turnover and £40m balance sheet operates a portfolio of commercial buildings. Quoted companies and large unquoted companies/LLPs are in scope; this entity qualifies. Required disclosures in the Directors' Report (or Energy and Carbon Report for LLPs): UK energy use (kWh) from gas, electricity and transport; associated Scope 1 and Scope 2 GHG emissions (tCO2e); at least one intensity ratio; methodology used (e.g. GHG Protocol); narrative on energy efficiency actions taken in the year; and prior-year comparatives after year 1. Quoted companies must additionally report global Scope 1+2 and material Scope 3. Low-energy exemption applies if total UK energy use ≤40 MWh. Filed with Companies House as part of annual report. Note: company size thresholds were uplifted by ~50% via the Companies (Accounts and Reports) (Amendment and Transitional Provision) Regulations 2024, effective for financial years starting on/after 6 April 2025.

question.text: A UK parent company has two German subsidiaries, each with ~300 employees and combined EU turnover of €180m. The board asks whether the group is in scope of CSRD via its EU subsidiaries, what the first reporting year is, and what assurance is required.

(2) The non-EU parent must itself publish a consolidated sustainability report where net EU-generated turnover exceeds EUR 150 million for two consecutive years and it has a qualifying EU subsidiary or branch, first for FY2028 published 2029. Two German subsidiaries of roughly 300 employees each meet the employee limb; whether each reports depends on meeting a second criterion. Timing for wave-2 entities is affected by the Stop-the-Clock provisions.

question.text: A commercial landlord in England has an EPC dated 15 March 2015 (Band E) for a 2,000 m² office. They want to grant a new 10-year lease on 1 July 2026. Is the existing EPC valid for the letting, what is the current MEES minimum, and what is the maximum civil penalty for non-compliance?

Current non-domestic MEES minimum is Band E (since 1 April 2018 for new lets; extended to all continuing lets from 1 April 2023). Maximum civil penalty for non-domestic MEES breach is £150,000 per property (or 20% of rateable value up to £150k for <3 months non-compliance; rising to £150k or 20% RV for ≥3 months) plus publication penalty. Proposed tightening to Band C from 1 April 2027 and Band B from 1 April 2030 remains unlegislated as of June 2026 — government formal response to the 2021 consultation still outstanding.

question.text: A landlord cannot economically improve a Band F non-domestic rental property in England to Band E because the cheapest qualifying measure has a payback exceeding the 7-year threshold. What MEES exemption can be registered, how long does it last, and what evidence must be uploaded to the PRS Exemptions Register?

answer.text: Register the 'all relevant energy efficiency improvements made' exemption or the '7-year payback' exemption on the PRS Exemptions Register (gov.uk). The 7-year payback exemption applies where no improvement satisfies the test that expected savings over 7 years ≥ cost of the measure. Exemption lasts 5 years from registration, after which the landlord must try again. Evidence required: three quotes from qualified installers for the relevant measure, the savings calculation (typically from the EPC recommendation report), property/landlord details, and a statement from the landlord. Exemption is not transferable on sale — the new owner must register their own exemption or comply. False registration is itself a breach attracting penalties up to £5,000 per misleading entry plus the underlying MEES penalty.

answer.text: Display Energy Certificates (DECs) are required for buildings >250 m² total useful floor area that are occupied by a public authority and frequently visited by the public (threshold lowered from 500 m² to 250 m² on 9 July 2015). DEC must be displayed in a prominent place clearly visible to the public. Penalty for failure to display: £500 fixed penalty; failure to possess a valid Advisory Report: £1,000. Enforcement by Trading Standards. DECs do not apply in Scotland (different regime under Section 63 of Climate Change (Scotland) Act / Assessment of Energy Performance of Non-Domestic Buildings (Scotland) Regulations 2016).

question.text: A facilities manager inherits a commercial office in England with 4 split air-conditioning units rated 15 kW each and one 60 kW VRF system. What TM44 air-conditioning inspection regime applies, what is the frequency, and what is the penalty for non-compliance?

answer.text: Total effective rated cooling output = (4 × 15) + 60 = 120 kW, which exceeds the 12 kW statutory threshold, so TM44 air-conditioning inspections are required. Inspections must be carried out at least every 5 years by an accredited energy assessor and the report lodged on the central EPB Register (Landmark). First inspection due within 5 years of installation, or by 4 January 2011 for systems already over 250 kW (now historic). Report must be given to the building operator/owner. Penalty for failure to commission/keep an inspection report: £300 fixed penalty per breach (per system), enforced by Trading Standards. Note this is the England & Wales regime; Scotland operates the same threshold under Energy Performance of Buildings (Scotland) Regulations 2008 as amended.

question.text: A landlord is marketing a non-domestic property in Scotland. How does the Scottish EPC regime differ from England & Wales, what is the Section 63 Action Plan trigger, and does MEES apply?

answer.text: Scottish EPCs are issued under the Energy Performance of Buildings (Scotland) Regulations 2008 (as amended), valid 10 years, lodged on the Scottish EPC Register operated by the Energy Saving Trust on behalf of Scottish Government (separate from the English Landmark register). Scotland uses a different methodology and rating scale presentation. The owner must then either implement improvements within 3.5 years or defer via annual operational ratings. MEES (the 2015 Regulations) does NOT apply in Scotland — Scotland has no equivalent minimum rating bar on letting as of June 2026, though the Scottish Government's Heat in Buildings Bill proposals include future non-domestic standards (not yet enacted).

question.text: A developer is planning a new district heat network serving 2,000 dwellings in Leeds, expected to be operational in 2027. Under the Energy Act 2023 and Ofgem's heat network regulatory framework, when does heat network authorisation become mandatory, who is the regulator, and what consumer protections apply?

question.text: A facilities manager is specifying a new 800kW air-cooled chiller for a commercial office in 2026. Under the UK F-Gas Regulation (retained EU 517/2014 as amended), what GWP restrictions apply to new stationary refrigeration/AC equipment, and what is the trajectory through 2030?

answer.text: Under the UK F-Gas Regulation (retained EU 517/2014, as amended by the Fluorinated Greenhouse Gases (Amendment) (EU Exit) Regulations 2019): single-split AC systems containing <3kg of F-gas with GWP ≥750 have been banned since 1 January 2025. Stationary refrigeration using HFCs with GWP ≥2500 banned since 2020 (with reclaimed/recycled exceptions to 2030). For an 800kW chiller (multi-split/centralised), no absolute GWP cap applies yet under the UK regime, but the HFC quota phase-down constrains supply: 2024-2026 quota is 31% of 2009-2012 baseline, dropping to 24% from 2027 and ~21% from 2030. Practical effect: R410A (GWP 2088) supply increasingly constrained; specify R32 (675), R454B (466), R1234ze (<1), or R290 where possible. NOTE: UK has NOT adopted the EU F-Gas Regulation 2024/573 which sets stricter caps (e.g. GWP <150 for some new chillers from 2027) - UK regime diverges and is under DESNZ review.

question.text: A heat network operator is setting tariffs for a new development with 500 domestic connections coming online in late 2026. answer.text: Under the Energy Act 2023 Part 8, Ofgem becomes consumer protection regulator for heat networks. question.text: A surveyor is advising on a Victorian tenement flat in Glasgow let on a Private Residential Tenancy. The landlord wants to know the current minimum EPC requirement in Scotland and the status of the proposed Section 63-style regime for non-domestic buildings. What are the current rules and proposed trajectory?

answer.text: Domestic PRS in Scotland: there is currently NO enforced minimum EPC band for private rented homes — the Scottish Government's proposed regulations requiring EPC C by 2025 (new tenancies) / 2028 (all tenancies) were paused in 2023. The Heat in Buildings Bill was withdrawn in 2024; a revised Heat in Buildings (Scotland) Bill was reintroduced in 2025 but as of June 2026 has not received Royal Assent. Non-domestic: Section 63 of the Climate Change (Scotland) Act 2009, implemented via the Assessment of Energy Performance of Non-domestic Buildings (Scotland) Regulations 2016, applies to non-domestic buildings >1,000 m² on sale or new lease — triggers an Action Plan requiring improvements within 3.5 years OR Display Energy Certificate operational rating monitoring. No proposed extension to domestic. Action: rely on existing 2016 Section 63 regime for non-domestic; assume domestic PRS standard remains uncertain.
answer.citation: Climate Change (Scotland) Act 2009 s.63; Assessment of Energy Performance of Non-domestic Buildings (Scotland) Regulations 2016; Heat in Buildings (Scotland) Bill 2025 (pending)

question.text: A public body in Wales (a local authority) is procuring a new secondary school. How does the Well-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act 2015 affect the procurement and design decision-making, and what specific carbon/EPC requirements apply under Welsh Building Regulations Part L (2022) compared with England?

answer.text: The Well-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act 2015 places a statutory duty on 44 listed public bodies (including local authorities and Welsh Ministers) to act in accordance with the sustainable development principle and to set well-being objectives reasonably contributing to the 7 national well-being goals (including 'A Resilient Wales' and 'A Globally Responsible Wales'). The Future Generations Commissioner can issue formal reviews; non-binding but politically significant. Procurement must apply the 5 ways of working (long-term, prevention, integration, collaboration, involvement). On Building Regs: Welsh Part L 2022 (in force 23 November 2022) requires a 37% CO2 reduction over Part L 2013 for new non-domestic buildings (and ~37% for new dwellings) — comparable headline to England's 27% (dwellings) / 27% (non-dom) but using a different notional building. No published date for a Welsh Future Buildings Standard equivalent to England's Future Homes Standard (in force 24 March 2027) — Welsh Government consultation 2024 indicated a 2026/27 trajectory but not yet laid as of June 2026.
answer.citation: Well-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act 2015; Building Regulations 2010 as amended by the Building (Amendment) (Wales) Regulations 2022; Approved Document L (Wales) 2022

question.text: An office building in Belfast is being sold. The seller asks whether an EPC is required, whether a Display Energy Certificate is needed, and how the Northern Ireland Energy Performance of Buildings regime differs from GB. What are the requirements and any MEES-equivalent restriction?

answer.text: Northern Ireland EPB regime: governed by the Energy Performance of Buildings (Certificates and Inspections) Regulations (Northern Ireland) 2008 (as amended). EPC required on construction, sale, or rent — valid 10 years — administered by the Department of Finance via Land & Property Services. EPC bands A–G as in GB but use SAP/SBEM 'NI' versions. DEC required for buildings >250 m² occupied by public authorities and frequently visited by the public (threshold reduced from 500 m² in line with EU EPBD recast, transposed in NI in 2013). Crucially: NI has NO Minimum Energy Efficiency Standard (MEES) — there is no equivalent of the England & Wales 2015 Regulations preventing letting of F/G properties, and no Section 63-style Action Plan regime. Letting an EPC G office in Belfast remains lawful as of June 2026. NI Executive's Energy Strategy (2021) signalled intent to consult on minimum standards but no regulations have been laid.
answer.citation: Energy Performance of Buildings (Certificates and Inspections) Regulations (Northern Ireland) 2008 (as amended 2013); NI Department for the Economy Energy Strategy 2021

Correct identification that NI has no MEES equivalent

question.text: A developer is proposing a 50-dwelling residential scheme. Compare the operational/embodied carbon planning requirements they will face if the site is in (a) the London Borough of Camden, (b) Cardiff, and (c) Edinburgh. What are the specific policy thresholds and assessment requirements?

answer.text: (a) Camden / London: London Plan 2021 Policy SI 2 requires major development (10+ dwellings) to achieve net-zero carbon, demonstrated via the energy hierarchy (Be Lean / Clean / Green) and a minimum 35% on-site CO2 reduction beyond Part L 2021 baseline (Building Regs 2021), with residual offset at £95/tCO2 over 30 years (GLA-set rate, periodically reviewed). Whole Life-Cycle Carbon Assessment mandatory for referable schemes (Policy SI 2 F) — generally 150+ homes or schemes referable to the Mayor. (b) Cardiff: Planning Policy Wales Edition 12 (Feb 2024) and TAN 12 require sustainable design; Cardiff LDP Policy KP16 sets sustainability targets but no fixed numeric carbon uplift beyond Welsh Part L 2022. No mandatory WLC assessment. (c) Edinburgh: City Plan 2030 (adopted 2024) Policy Sus 2 sets net-zero aspiration but enforcement relies on Scottish Building Standards Section 6 (2023) — currently ~32% CO2 reduction vs 2015 baseline; no statutory WLC threshold. Action: only London imposes hard offset price + WLC; Welsh/Scottish regimes rely primarily on Building Standards.
answer.citation: London Plan 2021 Policy SI 2; Planning Policy Wales Edition 12 (2024); City of Edinburgh Council City Plan 2030; Scottish Building Standards Technical Handbook Section 6 (2023)

question.text: A housing association is replacing gas boilers across its stock of social housing in Glasgow, Cardiff and Manchester. What current and proposed restrictions on fossil fuel heating apply in each jurisdiction in 2026, and when does each regime bite?

answer.text: Glasgow (Scotland): New Build Heat Standard in force since 1 April 2024 (via Building (Scotland) Amendment Regulations 2023) — prohibits direct emission heating systems in new buildings warranted from that date; does NOT apply to retrofit boiler replacement. Heat in Buildings (Scotland) Bill 2025 proposes restrictions on fossil heating in existing buildings but not yet enacted as of June 2026. Cardiff (Wales): Welsh Part L 2022 transitional rules effectively prevent gas in most new dwellings via fabric and primary energy targets; no current statutory ban on like-for-like boiler replacement in existing social housing. Optimised Retrofit Programme funding conditions favour heat pumps but are not regulatory. Manchester (England): Future Homes Standard comes into force 24 March 2027 — will end gas connections in NEW homes; no enacted ban on existing boiler replacement (the previous government's proposed 2035 phase-out of new fossil boilers was scrapped September 2023; Clean Heat Market Mechanism live from April 2025 places obligation on manufacturers, not landlords). Action: replacement gas boilers in existing social housing remain lawful in all three jurisdictions in June 2026.
answer.citation: Building (Scotland) Amendment Regulations 2023 (New Build Heat Standard); Approved Document L (Wales) 2022; Clean Heat Market Mechanism Regulations 2024; Heat in Buildings (Scotland) Bill 2025 (pending)
